items.readable_text:
Content:
The negation of the predicate [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is a new predicate that we denote as follows:
[MATH: \lnot P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)]
This predicate is true if and only if [MATH: P] is false for a specific set of assignment variables [MATH: x_1,x_2, \ldots x_n.]

Content:
For example, consider the following predicate defined over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb Z.]

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: P(m):] [MATH: m] is even

Content:
Then, [MATH: \lnot P(m)] is a new predicate that reads as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: m] is not even

Content:
This can be simplified as:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: m] is odd

Content:
For example:

Content:
- [MATH: P(2)] is true while [MATH: \lnot P(2)] is false
- [MATH: P(3)] is false while [MATH: \lnot P(3)] is true

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let [MATH: T_P] be the truth set of the predicate [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n).]

Content:
From the definition of the negation of a predicate, we have that [MATH: \lnot P] is true if and only if [MATH: P] is false. Therefore, the truth set of [MATH: \neg P] is the complement of the truth set of [MATH: P{:}]

Content:
[MATH: T_{\neg P} = \overline{T}_P]

Content:
For example, consider the following predicate defined over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb{R}{:}]

Content:
> [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: -2x +3 \leq 5]

Content:
To find the the truth set of [MATH: P(x),] we solve the inequality:

Content:
[MATH: − 2x + 3|≤ 5; − 2x|≤ 2; x|≥ − 1]

Content:
So, the truth set of [MATH: P(x)] is [MATH: T_P = [-1,\infty).]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: T_{¬P}|= T^(―)_{P}; = [− 1, ∞)^(―); = (− ∞, − 1).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The negation of the predicate [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)] is a new predicate that we denote as follows:
[MATH: \lnot P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)]
This predicate is true if and only if [MATH: P] is false for a specific set of assignment variables [MATH: x_1,x_2, \ldots x_n.]

Content:
For example, consider the following predicate defined over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb Z.]

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: P(m):] [MATH: m] is even

Content:
Then, [MATH: \lnot P(m)] is a new predicate that reads as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: m] is not even

Content:
This can be simplified as:

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: m] is odd

Content:
For example:

Content:
- [MATH: P(2)] is true while [MATH: \lnot P(2)] is false
- [MATH: P(3)] is false while [MATH: \lnot P(3)] is true

---

Item 2 — Example: Negating a Predicate Expressed in Plain English

[MATH: x]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The symbol "[MATH: \neg]" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence.

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:
[MATH: x]

In other words, [MATH: x] is smaller than [MATH: 10.] Therefore, [MATH: \neg P(x)] means the following:
[MATH: x]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Truth Sets of Negations

Content:
Let [MATH: T_P] be the truth set of the predicate [MATH: P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n).]

Content:
From the definition of the negation of a predicate, we have that [MATH: \lnot P] is true if and only if [MATH: P] is false. Therefore, the truth set of [MATH: \neg P] is the complement of the truth set of [MATH: P{:}]

Content:
[MATH: T_{\neg P} = \overline{T}_P]

Content:
For example, consider the following predicate defined over the universal set [MATH: \mathbb{R}{:}]

Content:
> [MATH: P(x):] [MATH: -2x +3 \leq 5]

Content:
To find the the truth set of [MATH: P(x),] we solve the inequality:

Content:
[MATH: − 2x + 3|≤ 5; − 2x|≤ 2; x|≥ − 1]

Content:
So, the truth set of [MATH: P(x)] is [MATH: T_P = [-1,\infty).]

Content:
Therefore, we have

Content:
[MATH: T_{¬P}|= T^(―)_{P}; = [− 1, ∞)^(―); = (− ∞, − 1).]

---
